notes.meaning: Moses worries that his own people will not believe God really appeared to him. God had already said they would listen (3:18), but Moses remembered how they had pushed him away before, and he feared it would happen again. His faith was weak but not gone, and God is patient with him. It had also been a very long time since God had appeared to anyone in Israel.

God asks a question not because He needs to know, but to make Moses look closely at what he holds. It is his plain shepherd's staff. God was about to use an ordinary tool from Moses's everyday life, not a king's sceptre.

The staff becomes a real snake, frightening enough that Moses runs. Then God tells him to grab it by the tail, which is the risky way to hold a snake. It took real faith to obey, and the snake became a staff again. The sign showed that a humble shepherd's stick, in God's hands, would make even proud Pharaoh afraid.
Here is the purpose of the sign. It would prove to the people that the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had truly sent Moses. The miracle also helped settle Moses's own heart about his calling.

Moses's hand turns white with leprosy, a skin disease people thought could not be cured. Then it is instantly healed. Only God could do that, so the sign showed God's power plainly. It also hinted that Moses would bring sickness on Egypt and see it lifted. And it reminded him that the power was God's, not his own.

God speaks as if the signs have a voice of their own. They speak clearly that Moses is God's messenger. If someone isn't convinced by the first sign, the second may persuade them. God kindly gives proof upon proof to help people who struggle to believe.

A third sign is held in reserve. Water from the Nile would turn to blood on the ground. Egypt depended on the Nile and even worshiped it, so this showed God could turn Egypt's greatest strength against it. Later the whole river would be turned to blood as a plague.

Now Moses says he is not a good speaker. He may have had some kind of speech problem, or he may have lost ease in the language after years away. Either way, a slow tongue does not mean a lack of wisdom. God often picks people with few natural advantages so that His grace shows more clearly.

God reminds Moses that He made the human mouth. He is Lord over every ability people have and every ability they lack. So Moses's weakness was no problem for Him. God rules over all of this in wisdom and for His glory.

God gives a direct order and a promise: "Go, and I will help you speak." He may not have removed Moses's weakness, but He would teach him what to say. Jesus made a similar promise to His followers (Matthew 10:19).
Every excuse has been answered, and now Moses's real problem comes out. He simply does not want to go. "Send someone else" is a curt and unwilling reply. It shows he was unwilling, not unable.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Many early church fathers read Moses's words as a prayer that God would send the promised Messiah now, since only He could do such a great work.

notes.meaning: God becomes angry. Even doubting yourself displeases Him when it keeps you from doing what He asks. Yet God does not reject Moses. He gives him his brother Aaron, a good speaker, who is already coming and will be glad to see him. Some think part of the honor, such as the priesthood, passed to Aaron because of this.

Moses will give Aaron the message, and Aaron will speak it to the people. Moses will be "like God" to Aaron. This means Moses is the one who receives God's word and tells Aaron what to say, the way God speaks through a prophet. God promises to help both of them, because even a gifted speaker needs God's help.
Moses must take the same shepherd's staff with him. It reminded him of his humble roots, and it would become his sign of authority. The miracles done with it would speak louder than any fine words.

Moses politely asks his father-in-law Jethro for permission to leave, since he worked for him. God's call did not cancel his duties to family. He did not tell Jethro about the vision at the bush, perhaps out of humility and good sense. Jethro kindly lets him go.
God reassures Moses that the men who wanted to kill him are dead. Moses may have had a hidden fear about going back, and God knew it. He knows how to calm our secret fears.

Moses sets out humbly, with his wife and sons on a donkey and himself on foot. In his hand is "the staff of God." It is called that because God's power would work through it. He looked poor, but he carried something greater than Pharaoh's might.

God tells Moses ahead of time that Pharaoh will not give in, so he won't be discouraged when the miracles seem to fail. God says He will harden Pharaoh's heart, which means making him stubborn. Traditional readers note that Pharaoh had already hardened his own heart against Israel's cries. God then hardened it further as a fair judgment.

differ.view: God hardened Pharaoh only after Pharaoh had hardened himself many times. God withdrew grace Pharaoh kept refusing and allowed him to go his own way, rather than putting evil in his heart.
God truly acted on Pharaoh's heart as a just judge, not merely by allowing it. We should speak as Scripture speaks and honor His judgments even when we can't fully understand them.
Some Baptists teach that God's hardening rests on His own purpose, not on anything Pharaoh did first.

notes.meaning: This is the first time anyone in the Bible says "This is what the LORD says." Prophets would later use those words often. God calls Israel His firstborn son, chosen and dearly loved. If Pharaoh will not free God's son to worship Him, Pharaoh will lose his own firstborn. That warning came true in chapter 12.

On the journey, God confronts Moses with deadly danger, perhaps through a sudden illness or an angel. The reason was that Moses had not circumcised his son. Circumcision was the sign God gave Abraham's family to mark them as His covenant people, and leaving it undone was serious. Moses had likely given in to his wife's dislike of the rite. Before he could lead God's people, he had to be faithful in his own home.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars see this as a very old story that describes God in human terms. They take "sought to kill him" as an old way of saying Moses became dangerously ill.

notes.meaning: Zipporah acts quickly. She circumcises her son with a flint knife and touches it to Moses's feet. Her words "bridegroom of blood" are hard to read. Some hear anger at the rite. Others hear that she won her husband back from death through her son's blood.

differ.view: Zipporah held up the blood to remind God of His promise. This points to Jesus, the true "Bridegroom of Blood," who stands between us and God's anger. Baptism has now taken the place of circumcision.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some suggest "bridegroom of blood" was once an old saying tied to circumcision before marriage.

notes.meaning: Once the neglected duty was done, God let Moses go and he recovered. When we turn back to God in obedience, He turns back to us in mercy. It seems Moses then sent his family back to Jethro for a time (see 18:2).

God sends Aaron to meet Moses, just as He promised in verse 14. They meet at the mountain where God had spoken to Moses. After about forty years apart, they greet each other with a kiss. Seeing God bring them together made the meeting even sweeter.
Moses tells Aaron everything God said and all the signs He gave. People who serve God together should share openly and work to understand each other fully.

The brothers gather Israel's elders, the older leaders of the people. Aaron speaks God's message, and the signs are done before them. The people were so worn down by suffering that they needed the miracles to help them believe.

Moses had feared rejection, but the people believed, just as God had said they would. They heard that God had seen their misery, and they bowed down and worshiped. Their faith would soon be tested and would waver. Still, this first welcome showed they were willing to follow God's call.
